title: Confirmation's gifts (CCC 1302–1305)
hookLine: it deepens baptismal grace, strengthens, and sends

lines: A LINE IN THE CENTER AISLE.
OIL, A CROSS, A FEW WORDS.
cards: A line forms in the center aisle. Teenagers in their best clothes, a few adults, each with a sponsor standing close behind, a hand on the shoulder. At the front, the bishop.
One by one they step up. He calls each by the name they've chosen, dips his thumb in oil, traces a cross on the forehead, says a few words about the gift of the Holy Spirit, and wishes them peace.
Afterward there are photos and cake. But the Catechism says something was given in that moment, and that it pushes outward.

teach.h: A SPECIAL OUTPOURING OF THE SPIRIT.
teach.b: Day one hundred twenty-seven met the oil and the seal; today, what they do.
The Catechism calls the effect of Confirmation a special outpouring of the Holy Spirit, like the one the apostles received at Pentecost, and it moves in three ways.
First, it deepens. Confirmation doesn't replace baptism; it brings baptismal grace to growth. It roots a person more deeply as a child of God, who can call God Father.
It unites them more firmly to Christ, and binds them more closely to the Church.
It increases the gifts of the Holy Spirit, gifts named from Isaiah's picture of the promised king, in the Douay-Rheims: "the spirit of counsel, and of fortitude."
Second, it strengthens: a special strength of the Spirit to spread and defend the faith in word and action, to confess Christ's name boldly, and never to be ashamed of the cross.

teach.h: IT SENDS, AND IT SEALS ONCE.
YOU SHALL BE WITNESSES UNTO ME.
teach.b: Just before the Ascension, in Acts, Jesus tells the apostles they'll receive the power of the Holy Spirit, "and you shall be witnesses unto me." That's the direction of the whole sacrament: out the door.
Like baptism, Confirmation is given only once. It leaves an indelible spiritual mark, a seal, a sign that Christ has claimed this person with his Spirit.
Quoting Thomas Aquinas, the Catechism says the confirmed receive the power to profess their faith publicly, almost as an official duty. So the oil on the forehead isn't an ending.
It's a sending, and the cake is the send-off.

how: In the Latin rite the bishop usually confirms, anointing the forehead with chrism; candidates choose a sponsor and often a saint's name. In the Eastern Catholic churches the sacrament, called chrismation, is given right after baptism.

games.q: you've just been confirmed. the oil is still on your forehead. according to the Catechism, what is this for?
o: to strengthen you to witness to Christ, in word and action.
to make you a member of the clergy.
games.why: the Catechism speaks of a special strength of the Spirit to spread and defend the faith, and never to be ashamed of the cross.

practice: Think of one place where you go quiet about something you care about: a table where you change the subject, a group chat where you don't type what you think, a friend you haven't been honest with.
If you pray, ask the Holy Spirit for courage there, in the Church's old words, Come, Holy Spirit, or in silence; if you don't, notice what courage would look like in that one place.

wordCard.voice: Confirmation's gifts. It deepens the grace of baptism, strengthens a person to witness, and sends them, sealed once and for good. Today's word.
